figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Cavewoman framework. The input-compression channel applies a deterministic part-of-speech filter to the user prompt at five reduction levels, leaving the system prompt fixed. The output-compression channel leaves the prompt verbatim and replaces the system prompt with a level-specific instruction that requires the same reduction in the response. Every generation is scored on task accuracy, reference-text agreement against the model’s unconstrained reference under bidirectional NLI (plus eleven complementary measures), and per-item input/output token cost.
figures.headline: Cavewoman applies the same five reduction levels to the prompt or the response, then scores every generation on accuracy, cost and agreement.
citing_sentences: Cavewoman holds $\mathcal{M}$ and $x$ fixed and applies the same reduction $\phi_{\ell}$ at one of two points (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Answer accuracy across the five reduction levels for all models and benchmarks. Solid bars denote input compression; hatched bars denote output compression. Significance markers indicate Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against the within-model unconstrained baseline (${}^{*}p{<}.05$, ${}^{**}p{<}.01$, ${}^{***}p{<}.001$). The dashed gold line marks the random-guessing baseline for each benchmark. Kimi-K2.6 is shown for completeness only and is excluded from all aggregates (Appendix E).
figures.headline: Input-compressed accuracy collapses at the strictest level, while output-compressed classification accuracy holds through deep levels.
citing_sentences: Input compression at the same reduction levels raises net cost on the remaining models (GPT-4o aside) before accuracy collapses at the strictest level (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Relative change in estimated per-item inference cost against the unconstrained baseline, averaged across the four API models. Left panel: input compression. Right panel: output compression. Rows are benchmarks; columns are the four non-zero reduction levels. Red denotes a cost increase, green a cost reduction. The two channels move in opposite directions at the same reduction level. Worst-case input-channel penalties reach $1.8\times$ at L1 and $\sim 2.7\times$ at deeper reductions (Finding 1).
figures.headline: Input compression raises average per-item cost at the same levels where output compression lowers it.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 reports the relative change in realized cost against the same-channel unconstrained baseline.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Per-model $2{\times}2$ dissociation at L1 output compression, summed across the five benchmarks. Each stacked bar partitions L1 output-compression generations into the four outcome cells: $C_{1}$ (correct + entails L0), $C_{2}$ (correct + does not entail L0), $C_{3}$ (wrong + entails L0), and $C_{4}$ (wrong + does not entail L0). Accuracy is $C_{1}{+}C_{2}$ and bidirectional NLI rate is $C_{1}{+}C_{3}$; the amber $C_{2}$ share is the dissociation. DeepSeek-R1 inverts the pattern. Kimi-K2.6 is shown for completeness only and is excluded from all aggregates (Appendix E).
figures.headline: For each non-reasoning model, correct but divergent answers are the largest off-diagonal share at first-level output compression, and the distilled reasoning model inverts this.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 resolves L1 output compression into its $2{\times}2$ outcome cells per model.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Per-level accuracy across the eight evaluated models and five benchmarks under both conditions. Solid: Condition A. Dashed: Condition B. The per-level bidirectional NLI grid is released alongside the artifact bundle.
figures.headline: Per-model accuracy curves across reduction levels show how accuracy changes under input and output compression for each benchmark.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 visualizes the accuracy data as per-model, per-dataset curves.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: $2\times 2$ dissociation by dataset, aggregated across L1–L3 and the eight evaluated models. Each panel shows Condition A and Condition B side by side; bar segments are the $C_{1}$–$C_{4}$ outcome shares.
figures.headline: Divergence shares are smaller on arithmetic benchmarks than on classification benchmarks in the per-benchmark breakdown.
citing_sentences: Table 13 aggregates L1 non-preservation by benchmark; Figure 6 breaks the $2\times 2$ dissociation down per-benchmark.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Mean accuracy, bidirectional NLI entailment against L0, and dissociation rate ($C_{2}$) for four input-compression configurations, averaged over the 3 models $\times$ 3 datasets the comparison was run on ($\tau{=}0.8$ is Qwen2.5-VL-7B only; see Table 17). $C_{2}>0$ under every method; the divergence reproduces beyond the POS filter.
figures.headline: All four input-compression methods keep the divergence above zero, so it persists beyond the part-of-speech filter.
citing_sentences: Table 17 and Figure 7 report cross-cell aggregates.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Worked example of the input-compression filter applied to a single question at each of the five reduction levels. L0 is the unmodified prompt; L1 removes closed-class function words; L2 retains nouns, verbs, and cardinal numerals; L3 strips the verbs to leave a nominal skeleton; L4 truncates the L3 form to its first fifteen tokens. The same filter family defines both channels.
figures.headline: A worked example traces one question through the five input-compression filters, from the full prompt to its first 15 tokens.
citing_sentences: Both the verbatim per-level filter rules (Condition A) and the verbatim per-level system prompts (Condition B) are listed in Appendix H. L4 is excluded from reference-text-agreement scoring since its Condition B system prompt asks the model to emit only the answer; the 15-token budget is conveyed as a prompt instruction rather than a hard decoder cap, and its soft-enforcement details are in Appendix G. A worked example of one question filtered through all five Condition A levels is in Appendix H (Figure 8).

abstract: “Talk short. Drop grammar. Save token.” This caveman style is widely promoted as a way to cut inference cost, but whether it actually saves anything depends on which channel (the user’s prompt or the model’s response) is being compressed. We present Cavewoman, a two-channel evaluation protocol that scores every generation on task accuracy, realized per-item cost, and reference-text agreement against the model’s unconstrained reference. We evaluate eight models on five datasets at five reduction levels, with both channels measured on the same items. Output compression cuts realized cost on most API models (1.4–2.4$\times$ per model, up to 3$\times$ in the best case) and on all four open-weight models under public-tier pricing. Input compression has the opposite effect, a strict lose-lose: it raises net cost rather than lowering it ($\approx 1.15\times$ on the five-benchmark mean, up to 1.8$\times$ on the worst dataset and 2.7$\times$ under stronger compression), because models compensate with longer responses even as accuracy collapses. Under the same setting, surface text diverges from the unconstrained reference: on the non-reasoning models, roughly half of all generations are correct yet their surface text no longer entails the model’s own unconstrained baseline generation. The divergence survives length-controlled re-scoring, multiple-comparisons correction, and replication under complementary semantic measures. Code and data are available at https://github.com/danielle34/cavewoman.

sections.body: Output tokens are priced 4–8× higher than input tokens. Existing methods compress either the prompt or the response, and usually report task accuracy at a reduced token count. The authors argue this cannot separate realized cost from prompt reduction, because a shorter prompt does not lower cost when the model answers at greater length. Cavewoman scores each generation on task accuracy, realized per-item cost, and reference-text agreement with the model's unconstrained generation. It applies five reduction levels to the input channel and to the output channel, with model and item held fixed. The panel covers eight models on GSM8K, BoolQ, ARC-Easy, CommonsenseQA and MMLU-STEM.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Accuracy at a reduced token count cannot separate realized cost from prompt reduction, so Cavewoman scores both channels on three axes.

sections.body: Input compression methods prune tokens by self-information, perplexity, question-aware scoring or distilled token classification, or encode prompts as soft vectors. Output methods constrain generation through length controls, budget-signalling encodings, countdown mechanisms, or prompting and post-training. The section notes that the content and function-word split used by the caveman register is long-standing in linguistics, yet this work reports only task accuracy at a token budget. Bidirectional entailment has been used to score summarization faithfulness and inter-system consistency. The closest prior work compresses one side only: LLMLingua on the input, and TokenSkip, Hansel and Sketch-of-Thought on the output. None measures whether the response says the same thing it would have said without compression.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior compression methods each reduce one channel and report accuracy at a token budget, and none checks reference-text agreement.

sections.body: The model and question are held fixed while a part-of-speech filter reduces them at five levels, L0 to L4. Condition A filters the user question under a neutral system prompt, so the model reads less. Condition B leaves the question intact and instructs the model to answer in the matching reduced register, so the model writes less. Per-level decoder budgets are 400, 300, 200, 150 and 20 `max_new_tokens`. Accuracy is regex-extracted, with a 0.01 tolerance on numeric answers. Reference-text agreement uses bidirectional entailment from a DeBERTa-based judge, replicated under eleven complementary criteria. Table 2 lists 11,465 items per model across the five datasets. L4 is excluded from semantic scoring because its Condition B prompt asks for the answer only.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Cavewoman holds the model and question fixed and applies five reduction levels to either the prompt or the response.

sections.body: Under output compression at the first level, realized cost falls by 1.4–2.4× per model on the three models that save, and by up to 3× in the best cell. Input compression raises cost: the telegraphic level reaches 1.8× on individual datasets and about 2.7× at deeper levels. Table 3 shows the mechanism. Input tokens fall while output tokens rise, so net cost is +15.4% for GPT-5.4 and +5.1% for Claude Sonnet 4.6, and −2.6% for GPT-4o. GPT-5.4 is cheaper on only two of its five benchmarks, because hidden reasoning tokens dominate its billed output. Across six non-reasoning models at the first output level, 51.9% of generations are correct yet no longer entail the unconstrained reference. Accuracy gains are reported only where unconstrained extraction is at least 0.95.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Output compression lowers realized cost on most API models while input compression raises it, and correct answers still diverge from reference text.

sections.body: Output is the channel to compress when a model answers at length. It yields cost savings on every API model whose billed output matches its visible response, while input compression does not. The section argues that accuracy under output compression does not follow from unconstrained accuracy: the highest-accuracy API model is least tolerant among the four API models. The divergence is a surface-text observation, not a propositional claim. Correctness is graded against the ground-truth answer, while agreement is graded against the model's own unconstrained generation. For deployments that consume only the final answer, the divergence does not affect outcomes. For transcripts, audit trails and reasoning displays, it does.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Single-axis evaluation is underdetermined, because cost, accuracy and reference agreement dissociate and a composite metric can mis-rank methods.

sections.body: Output compression cuts realized cost on most API models, by 1.4–2.4× per model and up to 3× in the best cell, and on all four open-weight models under public-tier pricing. Input compression raises net cost through compensatory output expansion, by up to about 15% on the five-benchmark mean and 1.8× on individual datasets, rising to 2.7× at deeper reductions. On the six-non-reasoning panel, 51.9% of generations are correct yet diverge from the unconstrained reference, and the divergence persists under length-controlled re-scoring. Stated limitations: the NLI judge measures surface text rather than propositional drift; all five benchmarks have short structured answers; decoding is greedy only; and the panel has two API vendors with two models each, so no vendor-level conclusion is drawn.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Candidates should be ranked at their deployment constraint level, since output-compression tolerance is not predicted by parameter count or unconstrained accuracy.

sections.body: The appendix gives May 2026 API prices, for example 2.50 USD and 10.00 USD per million input and output tokens for GPT-4o. The four open-weight models run on 2× NVIDIA L40S 48GB at bfloat16, about 425 GPU-hours in total. Table 6 lists dataset sizes, splits, mean L0 tokens and licenses. Inference is greedy, and only 0.9%, 7.3% and 0.9% of L1 Condition B outputs hit the ceiling for GPT-4o, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Projected open-weight savings at L1 Condition B are 2.5× for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 2.09× for Gemma-4-E4B. Under L4 Condition A, outputs average 19.8 tokens against a 15-token target.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists pricing, dataset statistics, inference configuration, token and cost accounting, constraint specifications, and released artifacts.
